title: Army Cleared to Detonate Volatile Bomb-Making Material in Iowa Following Court Ruling
snippet: A federal appeals court has paved the way for the U.S. Army to detonate 68 barrels of unstable lead azide in eastern Iowa, resolving legal delays despite local health anxieties and political friction.
content:
MIDDLETOWN, Iowa — Following days of legal wrangling, political friction, and mounting community anxiety, the U.S. Army is moving forward with plans to execute a controlled detonation of 68 barrels of highly volatile bomb-making material in southeastern Iowa on Wednesday morning.

The green light came late Monday after a three-judge panel of the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that an emergency permit issued by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) incorporated adequate safety measures to minimize the spread of hazardous lead dust.

A High-Stakes Race Against the Elements

The operation targets degraded lead azide—an extremely sensitive explosive compound widely used in military detonators—that was discovered earlier this year at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, located about 90 miles south of Cedar Rapids. Over time, the chemical has crystallized along the inside rims and lids of the storage drums, creating an extraordinarily dangerous situation where even minor friction could trigger a lethal blast.

In court filings, Army munitions experts stressed that rapidly dropping temperatures in Iowa significantly elevate the risk. As moisture inside the barrels freezes, the crystal formations become far more sensitive, making immediate disposal critical to avoiding an unintended explosion.

"The longer we wait, the longer the risk accumulates that they might have an accidental explosion," said John Goodpaster, a chemistry professor at Indiana University Indianapolis. Goodpaster noted that aging explosives present severe challenges for bomb technicians. "They are in a situation where they've got a large amount of very dangerous material and not very many good options."

Political Friction and Public Concern

The planned detonation has fueled debate that reached all the way to the White House. President Donald Trump threw an unexpected wrinkle into the saga on Monday, posting on social media that Governor-elect Rob Sand should weigh in on the decision. Sand, a Democrat who assumes office in January, swiftly responded that the call rests entirely with federal experts and the current administration, noting that prior neglect had left officials with "no good options."

Environmental watchdog group Earthjustice had initially secured a temporary stay against the blast, arguing that federal authorities failed to thoroughly evaluate safer chemical neutralization alternatives. While the appellate court ultimately permitted the Army to proceed under emergency authority, environmental advocates insist the military must provide surrounding communities with greater transparency and safety guarantees.

With the countdown underway, residents near Middletown are taking precautionary steps, sealing doors and windows to guard against potential airborne lead particles. EPA guidelines recommend that local residents remain indoors during the blast and wash down outdoor surfaces with water afterward. Meanwhile, officials in neighboring Missouri and Illinois have initiated independent air and water monitoring to track any potential environmental fallout.
